Bill
bil
noun
From the Middle English bille, through the Anglo-Latin billa, a variant of bulla, “a seal or sealed document”; hence any written instrument — a deed, a bond, an account of debt — whose force lies in its being written and delivered.

Biblical Definition

A bill in the Authorized Version is a written legal instrument: a document that fixes in ink what would otherwise be a man’s changeable word. It appears in two settings. The first is the marriage law, where the hard husband is required to “write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand” (Deu 24:1) — and the requirement is the mercy in it, for the writing takes time, the delivery is public, and the deed can never be recalled (Deu 24:4). The second is the counting-house, where the unjust steward calls in his lord’s debtors and says, “Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty” (Luk 16:6). There the bill is the record of what a man owes, and the whole force of the parable turns on the fact that a written obligation is a real one. Scripture then lifts the word. Isaiah has the LORD challenge His people to produce the deed of their mother’s severance: “Where is the bill of your mother’s divorcement, whom I have put away?” (Isa 50:1). No such paper exists. And in Jeremiah the LORD, having borne with backsliding Israel, says He “had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce” (Jer 3:8) — the covenant God who does nothing arbitrarily, whose severances are documented and just. Behind every biblical bill stands the truth that God keeps records.

Webster 1828 Definition

A written instrument — a deed, bond, or account of debt; in Scripture the bill of divorcement and the debtor’s bill, both binding because written.

expand to see more

BILL, a written paper containing a statement of particulars; an account of goods sold, or of debt due.

In law, a declaration in writing, expressing some wrong the complainant hath suffered, or a fault committed by some person.

A bill of divorce, a writing given by a husband to his wife, declaring the marriage dissolved (Deu 24:1).

From the Anglo-Latin billa, a variant of bulla, a seal — whence also the papal bull, a sealed instrument.

Distinguished from a bond by requiring no surety, and from a note by being a statement of particulars.

Key Scripture

Deu 24:1 — "When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found some uncleanness in her: then let him write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house."

Mar 10:4 — "And they said, Moses suffered to write a bill of divorcement, and to put her away."

Luk 16:6 — "And he said, An hundred measures of oil. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty."

Jer 3:8 — "And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed adultery I had put her away, and given her a bill of divorce; yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not, but went and played the harlot also."

Modern Corruption

The modern instinct treats the paperwork as the permission — if a thing can be lawfully filed, it must be lawfully done; Scripture makes the written deed a restraint upon sin, never a warrant for it.

expand to see more

The live corruption around this small word is the confusion of legality with lawfulness. Moses required a bill so that a man could not put away his wife in a fit of temper on a Tuesday and take her back on a Thursday; the document was friction, witness, and finality. The modern mind reads the same statute backwards and concludes that because the law provided a form, the law approved the act. Our Lord forecloses that reading exactly: Moses suffered it “because of the hardness of your hearts” (Mat 19:8; Mar 10:5). A permission granted to restrain an evil is not a blessing pronounced upon it. The same error runs through a hundred modern questions — the state issues a licence, files a certificate, stamps a form, and the conscience quiets itself on the strength of the stamp. But no civil registry can make lawful what God has forbidden, and no filed instrument can dissolve what God has joined (Mat 19:6).

The second corruption is subtler and belongs to the counting-house. The steward’s bills in Luke 16 are records of real debt, and his crime is that he alters them — fifty for a hundred, fourscore for a hundred — with another man’s goods. A culture that regards every written obligation as renegotiable, every contract as a starting position, every debt as a grievance, has learned the steward’s trade and forgotten his Lord’s ledger. Scripture’s comfort is not that the bill is fictitious but that it has been paid: the handwriting of ordinances that was against us Christ took out of the way, nailing it to His cross (Col 2:14). That is the only cancellation of a bill the gospel offers, and it cost blood. Recover the plain principle: a written word binds, God keeps accounts, and the debt is discharged by satisfaction, not by amendment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

English bill from Anglo-Latin billa, a sealed document; it renders Hebrew sēpher, a writing, and Greek gramma, a written thing.

expand to see more

Hebrew sēpher (H5612) — a writing, book, scroll, or legal document; in Deu 24:1 the sēpher kērīthūth, the writing of severance.

Greek gramma (G1121) — a letter, a written record; the steward’s grammata are the account-books of Luk 16:6–7.

Greek apostasion (G647) is also rendered “bill of divorcement” in Mar 10:4.

Anglo-Latin billa from bulla, a seal or boss — the seal, not the ink, was what once made a paper binding.

The Reformers seized the ledger figure gladly: Christ blots out the handwriting that stood against us (Col 2:14).

Usage

"Of the written deed of severance in the marriage law and in our Lord’s exposition of it (Deu 24:1; Mar 10:4)."

"Of a record of debt in the parable of the unjust steward, altered by a servant with his lord’s goods (Luk 16:6–7)."

"Figuratively of the LORD’s covenant dealings — the bill He gave backsliding Israel (Jer 3:8), and the bill Judah cannot produce (Isa 50:1)."
